title: Bouncing ball

reference.basis: plain white sheet taken as A4 at 0.210 x 0.297 m long side

slow_motion.evidence: No narration, captions, or on-screen text indicate slow motion.

subjects.description: small glossy red sphere falling and bouncing

observation.what_happens: A red ball drops from below a white paper taped to a wall down toward the brown floor. It bounces repeatedly with decreasing height, starting from rest near the paper and still bouncing when the clip ends.

calibration.note: white paper = 0.297 m (plain white sheet taken as A4 at 0.210 x 0.297 m long side) spans 171 px in SAM's mask

given: scale: white paper = 0.297 m (plain white sheet taken as A4 at 0.210 x 0.297 m long side) spans 171 px in SAM's mask, known to ±6%
reasoning: y shows near-parabolic free fall then a rebound to ~60% height and a second fall, while x drifts steadily, so motion is ballistic with a floor restitution event. Fall of ~0.52 m in ~1.3 s implies apparent g near 0.7 m/s2, far below 9.81, suggesting slow-motion video time, so g is left free wide. Candidates compete vacuum flight versus linear versus quadratic air drag, all with the same bounce, to test whether air shapes the unseen later bounces.

caveats: Scale assumes the paper is A4, good to about six percent, so absolute sizes and gravity share that uncertainty.
Fitted gravity is far below Earth normal, suggesting slow-motion footage, so treat it as effective timing.
The ball was still bouncing when the clip ended, so later bounces are untested.
critique.finding: The ball drops under gravity with g = {g} and bounces off the floor at {y_floor}. Each bounce keeps {e} of its falling speed, so hops get lower.
critique.headline: Ball falls freely, rebounds losing energy each bounce.
critique.why_it_won: The winner captures every rebound with just gravity and a bouncy floor, while adding air drag does nothing extra.

headline: Ball falls freely, rebounds losing energy each bounce.
finding: The ball drops under gravity with g = 0.593 ± 0.036 m/s² and bounces off the floor at -0.543 ± 0.033 m. Each bounce keeps 0.78 ± 0.00029 of its falling speed, so hops get lower. That is 17× weaker than Earth’s gravity, so the clip most likely plays about 4.1× slower than real life.

eyeball.confidence: low - only first frame visible, scale from paper and timing inferred
eyeball.law_in_words: vertical free fall with constant gravitational acceleration in video time, followed by a partially inelastic bounce at the floor with vertical restitution e

clock.note: Gravity came out 17× too weak. Either this happened somewhere with 0.06× Earth’s gravity, or the clip plays about 4.1× slower than real life (slow motion). Run it again with the slow-motion factor set.
